national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — federal authority for corporate income tax, GST/HST, payroll, and excise; official portal: My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/digital-services-businesses/business-account.html). Provincial counterpart for Quebec: Revenu Québec (RQ) — official portal: Mon dossier d'entreprise (https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/on-line-services/for-businesses/), administering QST (Quebec Sales Tax / TVQ), Quebec corporate income tax, and provincial source deductions. Federal incorporation registry: Corporations Canada (ISED); Quebec enterprise registry: Registraire des entreprises du Québec.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A Quebec Business Corporation obtains its nine-digit federal Business Number (BN) automatically upon federal incorporation through Corporations Canada, or upon extra-provincial registration of a foreign corporation with the Registraire des entreprises. The BN serves as the master tax identifier; program accounts are appended as prefixes (e.g., RT+BN for GST/HST, RC+BN for payroll, RP+BN for Quebec source deductions). Activation/registration is done through CRA My Business Account or Forms RC1 (resident) / RC1W (non-resident), including GST/HST program account activation. For GST/HST, registration is mandatory once taxable supplies in Canada exceed C$30,000 over a four-calendar-quarter period (or C$30,000 in a single quarter), except that non-resident suppliers of specified digital products and services (e.g., downloadable video games delivered electronically) are required to register without a Canadian 'carrying-on-business' nexus if they are not a small supplier. The corporation must separately register with Revenu Québec for QST: registration with RQ (QST number with prefix TQ/RM) is mandatory when the corporation is not a small supplier (C$30,000 threshold) and makes taxable supplies in Quebec; digital-service and e-commerce suppliers to Quebec consumers are subject to QST registration under Quebec's destination-based place-of-supply rules, with no permanent-establishment requirement. The same BN must be referenced in the Registraire des entreprises annual declaration and all provincial tax filings.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No U.S.-style check-the-box election exists under the Canadian Income Tax Act; a Business Corporation is automatically a Canadian-resident taxpayer subject to entity-level tax on worldwide income (with Quebec provincial allocation via permanent establishment). Available statutory elections relevant to digital publishing: (i) GST/HST closely related corporation election under ETA s.156 to treat intercorporate supplies as made for nil consideration and outside GST/HST (subject to carve-outs for real property, financial services, and regulated supplies); (ii) corresponding QST election under the Quebec Taxation Act (LQV s.21.1.1) for supplies between closely related corporations; (iii) deemed-supplier election for a resident agent acting for a non-resident principal; (iv) ETA s.156(3) election to treat a member of a corporate group as the single registrant; (v) income tax rollover elections (ITA s.85, s.87 amalgamation, s.88 winding-up), foreign affiliate elections (ITA s.93), and Canadian-controlled private corporation elections for the small business deduction; (vi) hybrid mismatch rules: Canada does not permit hybrid entity classification elections for Canadian corporations, but applies the excessive interest and financing expenses limitation (EIFEL) provisions (ITA s.18.2/18.4) and hybrid mismatch arrangement rules to deny deductions for hybrid-financing payments, including where a Canadian payer is treated as pass-through in a foreign jurisdiction.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (federal value-added tax) and QST (Quebec Sales Tax / TVQ, a provincial value-added tax administered by Revenu Québec); the Province of Quebec applies a destination-based VAT architecture with input tax refund mechanics for QST mirroring GST/HST ITCs.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: C$30,000 (CAD) small-supplier threshold for GST/HST — measured on total taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) made in Canada during the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters, or more than C$30,000 in a single calendar quarter; financial services are excluded. Non-resident suppliers of specified digital products/services (including software downloads and game publishing rights via online marketplaces) are deemed to make taxable supplies in Canada and must register unless they qualify as small suppliers; CRA guidance GI-084 measures the threshold on worldwide taxable revenues of non-residents. For QST, Revenu Québec applies an equivalent C$30,000 small-supplier threshold; non-resident digital-supply providers and e-commerce platform operators marketing to Quebec consumers must register for QST from the first taxable sale if not a small supplier.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, continuous transaction control, or government pre-clearance e-invoicing mandate exists for B2B or B2C transactions in Canada or Quebec; the CRA accepts standard tax invoices containing prescribed registrant, description, consideration, and tax-disclosure particulars. Canada is progressively adopting OECD interoperative e-invoicing frameworks (PEPPOL BIS 3.0) for business-to-government procurement; Revenu Québec mandates electronic invoicing for suppliers contracting with Quebec public bodies, with phased implementation from 2025 applying to large suppliers. For Steam/PlayStation digital sales, the marketplace operator (Valve / Sony Interactive Entertainment) is statutorily responsible, under Canada's marketplace rules and Quebec's platform rules, for charging, collecting, and remitting GST/HST and QST on taxable supplies of digital products to Canadian consumers facilitated through the platform; the publishing corporation must maintain complete platform settlement statements, marketplace tax certificates, and per-territory revenue reports to support its own GST/HST and QST filing positions and zero-rating of non-Canadian sales.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available under ETA Schedule VI, Part V, generally for (i) supplies of goods exported by the supplier from Canada (s.5), (ii) supplies of intangible personal property (IPP) made to a non-resident person who is not registered for GST/HST and not using the IPP in Canada (s.21), and (iii) services supplied to non-residents where the service does not relate to real property in Canada, tangible personal property located in Canada, or an individual present in Canada (s.7). QST zero-rating for Quebec suppliers parallels the GST/HST rules under the Regulation respecting the QST (s.8 et seq.; Revenu Québec interpretation MP-62-5R). For PC/console game publishing through Steam and PlayStation Store, the publisher may zero-rate: (a) the supply of digital publishing/exploitation rights (IPP) paid by Valve/Steam or Sony (non-resident platform operators), provided the rights are not exploited in Canada and the operators are not GST/HST registrants in relation to those rights; and (b) end-user software downloads digitally delivered to non-resident consumers outside Canada, demonstrated by recipient IP geolocation, billing address, store-region code, payment instrument country, and PSN/Steam account residency. The supply is taxable at 5% GST plus 9.975% QST only where the recipient's usual place of residence is Canada (Quebec for QST); server location and platform payout location are irrelevant to place of supply.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (Canada Border Services Agency export declaration via eHUB/CAED for any physical carrier media, merchandise, or promotional goods exported; not applicable to intangible electronic downloads)
Bill of Lading (outward ocean/air waybill or courier proof of export for physical game media or merchandise)

Inward Remittance Certificate (for digital payouts, the Steam/Valve treasury settlement report and PlayStation Store payout statement along with correspondent bank beneficiary credits constitute the FX-repatriation evidence; Canada imposes no statutory inward remittance certificate requirement)
Platform settlement reports and payout advisories from Steam/Valve and PlayStation Store clearly segregating Canadian and non-Canadian sales
Master publishing, distribution, and IP-licence agreements evidencing the non-resident recipient and contractual place of supply

Digital supply metadata logs (IP address geolocation, device identifier, download/activation timestamps, store-region codes, payment-card country codes) demonstrating delivery or making available outside Canada
Intercompany or agency agreements where a foreign commissionaire, distributor, or marketplace operator facilitates the zero-rated export supply
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Canada has no statutory 180-day FX repatriation deadline under tax law; the 180-day benchmark is an internal compliance control aligned with Steam/Valve and PlayStation payment cycles and prudent corporate treasury practice. CRA and Revenu Québec audit zero-rated digital exports aggressively through international e-commerce programs (E-audit, data-mining of platform settlement data, OECD/MLC information sharing). If zero-rating is claimed without adequate proof of non-residence and foreign delivery, the authorities may reassess GST/HST (and QST) at the full 14.975% combined rate on all platform revenues, deny corresponding input tax refunds, and apply: (i) a 25% penalty on amounts owing for willful participation or culpable conduct (ETA s.281.1; QST equivalent under LQV), (ii) a 20% gross-negligence penalty for false statements or omissions (ITA s.163.2), (iii) interest at prescribed rates compounded daily, (iv) retrospective reassessment windows of 4 years (10 years in cases of misrepresentation or fraud), and (v) in egregious cases, criminal prosecution for evasion (ETA s.328 / ITA s.239) with fines up to 200% of the tax evaded and imprisonment up to five years. For Quebec, Revenu Québec penalties and seizure powers apply independently. A publishing corporation should retain zero-rating evidence (platform reports, geolocation logs, contracts, and payout reconciliation) for at least six years from the end of the relevant reporting period, and for seven years where any dispute is pending or expected.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as monetary authority and supervisor of retail payments under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) since 2024; exchange control is not centralized in Canada. Regulatory oversight is distributed among the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for AML/ATF and wire reporting, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for tax-related cross-border compliance. There is no dedicated Foreign Exchange Administration; the Canadian dollar is a fully floating currency and no emergency exchange-control machinery is currently in force.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada provides full current-account and capital-account convertibility. No exchange-control approvals, no surrender quotas, and no minimum holding periods apply to capital injections, dividends, royalties, or liquidation proceeds. Profit remittance to non-residents is subject only to Part XIII withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (Canada) (statutory rate 25%; generally 15% for arm's-length direct recipients and 5% for a US corporate parent under the Canada–US Income Tax Convention, with a refund/relief mechanism available). Practical hurdles are bank-and-tax-driven: FINTRAC Electronic Funds Transfer Reports (EFTR) for cross-border wires at or above CAD 10,000; CRA Form T106 information returns for reportable non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents; thin-capitalization documentation for shareholder loans under ITA section 18(4); and applicable Quebec financial administration filings for a Quebec-incorporated publisher.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: No statutory export-proceeds surrender requirement and no mandatory conversion ratio exist in Canada. Steam and PlayStation Store payouts may lawfully be retained in USD, held in foreign-currency bank accounts, or converted at market rates. The relevant obligations are: (a) FINTRAC reporting for incoming/outgoing electronic funds transfers at or above CAD 10,000 and Large Cash Transaction Reports at or above CAD 10,000; (b) record-retention requirements under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA); (c) CRA foreign-currency translation for income computation using Bank of Canada published exchange rates; and (d) CBSA cross-border currency and monetary instruments reporting (Form E677) for physical movement of funds at or above CAD 10,000.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Rated Medium for operational sub-accounts only. Foreign digital EMIs (for example Wise, Airwallex, Mercury, or Payoneer) may lawfully service a Quebec corporation if they are registered with FINTRAC as a money services business or foreign money services business and, when engaging in retail payment activities, are licensed by the Bank of Canada under the RPAA. A foreign EMI cannot replace a Tier-1 Schedule I bank for treasury-critical functions: it has no access to Lynx (CAD RTGS), no Canadian clearing code for direct CAD settlement, no CDIC deposit insurance, and platform payout agreements with Valve/Steam and Sony PlayStation typically require a regulated commercial bank account. Recommended treasury architecture: maintain the Tier-1 Canadian bank operating account as the master treasury node; use USD-denominated EMI sub-accounts strictly for collecting Steam/PlayStation proceeds with same-day sweeping into the Canadian regulated account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical attendance is not a statutory mandate under Canadian or Quebec law, but most Quebec-based relationship managers require at least one in-branch interview at the Montreal or Quebec City location for the legal representative or a resident director. Non-resident directors may be onboarded using remote video attestation supported by notarized identification and apostilled corporate documents, but approval timelines materially increase. Optimal approach: appoint a resident director and complete onboarding in two to five business days. National Bank of Canada and RBC accept hybrid remote/in-branch verification for low-risk software publishers with a complete FINTRAC-aligned compliance file; smaller cooperative institutions may insist on fully physical presence.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident director or offshore beneficial-owner concentration without meaningful Canadian nexus, resulting in shell-company profiling and automatic account refusal.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified Certificate of Incorporation (Corporations Canada or Registraire des entreprises du Québec); updated Articles and By-laws; full beneficial-ownership register; Quebec commercial lease and utility invoices; payroll evidence including Relevés des employés filings; notarized board resolutions designating authorized signatories; biometric identification of each director; shareholder subscription agreements with source-of-funds statements.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume digital-store proceeds from Valve/Steam and PlayStation Store flagged as low-entry-barrier e-commerce flows, triggering enhanced FINTRAC/PIPEDA scrutiny of money-laundering exposure.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed Steamworks and PlayStation Partner publishing agreements; platform payout statements and net-revenue reports; treasury flow chart demonstrating arms-length storefront remittances; written AML/ATF program with designated compliance officer; transaction-monitoring policy; audited or reviewed financial statements; dual-signatory board authorization for all wire destinations.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: USD account requests and cross-border wire volumes causing EFTR density and suspicion of undisclosed foreign trusts, tax-haven conduits, or unregistered foreign assets.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Board resolutions documenting FX hedging policy and treasury mandate; ISDA or bank-standard FX master agreement status; evidence of underlying receivables from platform net-revenue reports; CRA Form T106 compliance matrix; Part XIII withholding-tax tracking for royalty outflows; declarations of non-resident shareholding; five-year bank references from prior financial institutions.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions-list or politically exposed persons (PEP) screening hit in the shareholder or director base, triggering automatic rejection under OSFI sanctions policy and PCMLTFA vetting frameworks.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Up-to-date OSFI/UN Consolidated List sanctions screening results for all shareholders, directors, and signatories; negative-media and PEP-search reports aged less than 30 days; biometric identity documents with proof of residential address; sworn affidavit on source of capital and wealth; independent legal opinion on beneficial-ownership transparency; written commitment to annual re-screening and immediate disclosure of ownership changes.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Execute SWIFT MT103 (customer credit transfer) in CAD to the Tier-1 Canadian operating account using institution/transit/final-account identifiers per Lynx routing standards, or in USD to the designated USD clearing account with the MT103 narrative specifying 'EQUITY CONTRIBUTION / SHARE SUBSCRIPTION' or 'SHAREHOLDER LOAN'. No Bank of Canada or OSFI approval letter is required. The receiving bank will require the board resolution authorizing issuance or borrowing, the share subscription agreement, and FINTRAC EFTR documentation where the value is at or above CAD 10,000. For shareholder loans exceeding the 2:1 debt-to-equity thin-capitalization threshold, interest deductibility is restricted under ITA section 18(4); document the loan agreement and, for non-resident lenders, verify Part XIII withholding obligations at the applicable treaty rate.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing rails: (i) SWIFT MT103 for USD/EUR vendor and middleware-royalty wires covering Unreal Engine, Unity, localization, and distribution partners; (ii) CAD domestic disbursements via Lynx (LVTS) RTGS through the Tier-1 bank, with overnight sweeps to interest-bearing treasury positions; (iii) USD in-Canada clearing via Fedwire/CHIPS through the Canadian bank's US correspondent network; and (iv) EUR via SEPA/TARGET2 for European platform payments. Commercial letters of credit are not standard for digital game publishing; the practical settlement method is open-account trading supported by MT103 wires, platform invoices, and automated reconciliation. Royalty payments to non-resident licensors must integrate CRA NR4 reporting and Part XIII withholding at the applicable treaty rate; Valve and Sony recoupment obligations should be processed through priority-sweep instructions to protect the commercial waterfall.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD FX forwards with terms from 1 to 24 months under bank balance-sheet or dealer facilities
CAD/USD FX swaps combining spot and forward legs for rolling hedge tenors
Vanilla CAD/USD FX options and zero-cost collars protecting the USD revenue floor
Cross-currency interest-rate swaps (CAD/USD) for matched balance-sheet exposure on multi-year platform receivables

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) permissible only as fallback instruments with offshore counterparties, noting that the Canadian dollar is fully convertible and deliverable forwards are the standard regulation-preferred hedging tool

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Enterprise Declaration (Déclaration annuelle) of the Registraire des entreprises
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the corporation's registration anniversary each year (anniversary-based calendar)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late fee C$30 (≈US$22) added to the C$30 base fee; after formal default notice and a 60-day rectification period, REQ administratively strikes off (dissolves) the enterprise and publishes the dissolution in the enterprise register.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal income tax)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after the end of the taxation year (fiscal year-end); federal tax balance generally due within 2 months, or 3 months for a Canadian-controlled private corporation with qualifying business income
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per full month of delinquency (maximum 12 months); gross-negligence penalty of 50% for false statements or omissions; compound daily interest; continued non-compliance may result in demand letters, garnishment, enforcement seizures, and prosecution.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Quebec Corporate Income Tax Return (CO-17 / CO-17-T)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after the end of the taxation year; provincial tax balance generally due within 2 months after fiscal year-end, or 3 months for a Canadian-controlled private corporation with taxable business income
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Penalty of 5% of unpaid provincial tax plus 1% per full month of delinquency (maximum 12 months); 50% penalty for misrepresentation; compound daily interest; continued non-compliance may trigger asset seizure, garnishment, and permit or tax-credit suspension.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Combined GST/HST and QST sales tax return under the SME single-administration agreement
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Revenu Québec (administers federal GST/HST for Quebec-based small businesses with worldwide taxable sales under C$30M); Canada Revenue Agency retains federal remittance authority above that threshold
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annual filing permitted when annual taxable worldwide revenues do not exceed C$1.5M (non-financial services, subject to Ministerial course); return and remittance due within 3 months after fiscal year-end; monthly or quarterly filings otherwise
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file or remit: penalty of 5% of unpaid net tax plus 1% per full month (maximum 12 months), compound daily interest, and potential Ministerial assessment; persistent default may lead to seizure, set-off against refunds, suspension of remittance accounts, and offense penalties.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No revenue or asset threshold imposes an automatic audit for private Business Corporations (Inc./Corp.); an independent audit is mandatory for reporting issuers (public and distributing corporations), corporations whose shareholders do not unanimously waive the auditor appointment, and entities required by CRA or Revenu Québec to provide audited financial statements in the context of tax verification or administration.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS is mandatory for publicly accountable enterprises; Canadian private enterprises apply ASPE (Part II of the CPA Canada Handbook) with the option to elect IFRS; both frameworks are accepted for CRA T2 and Revenu Québec CO-17 filings, with reconciled schedule M/M-related adjustments applied in tax computations.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The annual REQ declaration serves as the recurring confirmation event for corporate information (name, head office, directors). Any share transfer or change of beneficial control must be recorded in the register of members and, when it alters information in the public declaration, must be reported to the Registraire des entreprises within 30 days of the change. Where the corporation is subject to the CBCA Significant Individuals regime (effective January 22, 2024), the private corporation must maintain an internal Significant Individuals / UBO register, update it within 15 days of any change, and confirm its accuracy at the time of the federal annual return.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (shareholder and director meetings and written resolutions)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: US$110–US$220 per year (Quebec registered office and registered agent service market range)
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: US$8,000–US$25,000 for an independent audit if not waived; US$2,500–US$6,500 for an accountant-compiled statement with a unanimous audit waiver

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Federal general corporate income tax rate: 15%. Quebec general corporate income tax rate: 11.5%. Combined general rate: 26.5%. For an eligible Canadian-controlled private corporation, the federal small-business rate is generally 9% and the Quebec rate is generally 3.2%, producing a combined rate of approximately 12.2% on qualifying active business income within the applicable business limit.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Eligible Canadian-controlled private corporations may access the federal small business deduction on qualifying active business income up to the applicable federal business limit, generally CAD 500,000 subject to associated-corporation and taxable-capital restrictions. Quebec provides a small-business deduction subject to Quebec eligibility and activity requirements. Scientific research and experimental development credits may apply to qualifying Canadian R&D expenditures; the federal general SR&ED investment tax credit is generally 15%, with enhanced rates potentially available to qualifying corporations. Quebec R&D credits may also apply. Canadian digital-media and production incentives are fact-specific and generally require prescribed activities, Canadian labour expenditure, certification, and filing documentation. Dividends received from foreign or Canadian affiliates, foreign exchange gains, withholding taxes, and digital-store commissions require separate tax characterization. Tax holidays are not generally available to an ordinary game publisher solely because it operates in Quebec.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, including applicable schedules, filed electronically through CRA-approved corporate tax software or the CRA Corporation Internet Filing service where available. Quebec provincial return: CO-17, Déclaration de revenus des sociétés, filed through Revenu Québec-approved electronic transmission. A corporation carrying on business in Quebec generally files both T2 and CO-17.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual income tax return; tax installments are generally monthly, or quarterly where the corporation satisfies the statutory installment conditions. GST/HST and Quebec QST returns are separate indirect-tax filings and may be monthly, quarterly, or annual.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 and CO-17 are generally due six months after the end of each taxation year. Corporate tax balances are generally due two months after year-end; an eligible Canadian-controlled private corporation may qualify for a three-month balance-due date if the applicable statutory conditions are met. Monthly installments are generally due on the last day of each month. Quebec and federal filing deadlines must be calculated independently where payment, installment, or electronic-filing rules differ.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number, corporation type, taxation-year start and end dates, Quebec permanent establishment status, principal business activity, and corporate mailing address.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-owned Canadian corporation must report its Canadian legal status and Canadian taxation year. Ownership, residency, associated corporations, and permanent establishments must be reported accurately; foreign ownership does not by itself make the Canadian corporation non-resident.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of accounting net income or loss to income for tax purposes, including non-deductible expenses, capital cost allowance, reserves, provisions, and other tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reverse accounting expenses that are not deductible under Canadian law. Digital-store commissions, platform fees, royalty expenses, related-party service charges, and foreign exchange items require supporting contracts and arm's-length analysis.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance by class for depreciable property, including computer equipment, servers, leasehold improvements, and qualifying software or intangible assets.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Classify software, hardware, development costs, and capitalized platform assets under the correct CCA classes. Separate current expenses from capital expenditures and maintain acquisition, disposal, and available-for-use evidence.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Related and associated corporations, ownership percentages, jurisdiction of residence, and allocation of business limits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose foreign parents, subsidiaries, sister companies, and corporations under common control. Associated-corporation status can reduce or eliminate access to the small-business limit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information concerning foreign affiliates, where applicable, including ownership and transactions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Complete the schedule where the Canadian corporation owns or is deemed to own relevant foreign affiliates. Review foreign accrual property income, surplus accounts, reporting, and repatriation consequences.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Shareholder information for shareholders owning specified ownership interests, including name, address, residency, and share information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify non-resident corporate or individual shareholders and retain beneficial-ownership records. Do not report nominee or intermediary information inaccurately.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income statement information by financial-statement category, including revenue, cost of sales, operating expenses, finance costs, and net income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report gross platform receipts and separately identify Valve, console-store, payment-processing, refunds, chargebacks, marketing, royalty, and related-party charges. Reconcile reported revenue to platform statements and bank receipts.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: General Index of Financial Information, including balance-sheet and income-statement data and accounting-policy information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use financial statements prepared consistently with the corporation's books. Intercompany balances, shareholder loans, accrued royalties, and foreign-currency balances must reconcile to agreements and confirmations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Schedule 9 identifies related and associated corporations. Form T106 reports non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents, generally where the aggregate reportable transaction category exceeds CAD 1,000,000 for the year or another statutory reporting condition applies.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report cross-border royalties, interest, management fees, development services, IP licenses, reimbursements, receivables, payables, and non-cash transactions. The T106 threshold does not remove the arm's-length pricing or contemporaneous-documentation requirement.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal investment tax credit information and provincial or territorial tax-credit information, including eligible SR&ED expenditures where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only qualifying Canadian expenditures supported by project records, technical narratives, employee time records, contractor evidence, and cost allocation schedules. A non-resident shareholder does not independently disqualify a Canadian corporation, but ownership and control can affect rates and credits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: CO-17 corporate income and capital tax fields
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quebec taxable income, Quebec allocation, taxable capital, business limit, refundable and non-refundable credits, installments, and balance payable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income to Quebec using the applicable Quebec allocation rules and disclose Quebec permanent-establishment facts. Reconcile CO-17 taxable income with T2 amounts and explain federal-provincial differences, credits, and interprovincial or international allocation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 5 and CO-17 related-party disclosures
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Interest, dividends, management fees, rents, royalties, and other amounts paid or payable to related persons, including withholding-tax and deductibility information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Verify treaty entitlement, beneficial ownership, withholding, remittance, NR4 reporting, and transfer-pricing support before deduction. Gross-up provisions and withholding obligations must be addressed contractually.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: For a late federal T2 return, the ordinary penalty is generally 5% of the unpaid tax balance plus 1% of that balance for each complete month late, up to 12 months; higher penalties may apply after a prior demand or repeated failure. Quebec generally imposes a 5% late-filing penalty plus 1% per month, subject to statutory limits. Interest on unpaid tax and installments is compounded daily at the prescribed rate. Gross-negligence penalties may generally equal 50% of the understated tax or overstated credit, and false statements or omissions can create additional penalties. Failure to file T106, foreign-affiliate information, or required slips can trigger separate fixed or formula-based penalties.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal T2 installment and balance-payment obligations through CRA My Business Account, CRA-authorized electronic payment channels, or financial institutions; Quebec payments through Revenu Québec's online services or approved banking channels.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Monthly installments by default; quarterly installments may be available to qualifying corporations. This is a payment obligation rather than a substitute for the annual T2 or CO-17 return.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Monthly installments are generally due on the last day of each month. A qualifying corporation may pay quarterly installments on the last day of each quarter. The balance-due date is generally two months after year-end, with a possible three-month date for an eligible Canadian-controlled private corporation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: CRA corporation account and payment period
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business number, corporation income-tax program account, taxation year, payment amount, and payment date.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the Canadian corporation's own business number and tax account. Do not pay through the foreign parent account or offset foreign tax against Canadian installments without a statutory basis.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Quebec corporation account and payment period
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quebec identification number, taxation year, installment period, and payment amount.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Maintain separate Quebec payment records and reconcile federal and Quebec installments to the current-year tax provision and prior-year assessments.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Installment interest and possible installment penalties apply where required installments are late or insufficient. Payments are credited according to CRA or Revenu Québec allocation rules; an incorrect account, late bank processing, or foreign transfer delay does not generally eliminate statutory interest.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: NR4 Statement of Amounts Paid or Credited to Non-Residents of Canada and NR4 Summary, filed with the CRA; related withholding remittances are made through the non-resident tax account.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual information return, with withholding remittances generally monthly.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: NR4 slips and the NR4 Summary are generally due by the last day of March following the calendar year. Amounts withheld from non-residents are generally remitted by the 15th day of the month following the month of payment or credit, subject to the corporation's remitter status and specific rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the legal name, foreign address, and residency information of the actual beneficial recipient. Retain ownership and beneficial-ownership evidence where an intermediary receives payment.
Use the foreign tax identification number or Canadian identification number where required and available.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross income paid or credited to the non-resident.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report the gross amount before withholding, including dividends, interest, royalties, and other prescribed Canadian-source amounts.
Report the actual amount withheld and remitted. Apply a treaty rate only after obtaining sufficient residency, beneficial-ownership, limitation-on-benefits, and treaty-eligibility evidence.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late, incorrect, or missing information returns may attract fixed penalties based on the number of slips and days late. Failure to withhold or remit can create personal liability for responsible directors and officers under the Income Tax Act, together with interest and penalties.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Canadian Part XIII withholding tax on taxable dividends paid or credited to a non-resident, subject to reduction under an applicable tax treaty. Common treaty rates are 5% where the corporate recipient satisfies the required ownership threshold and 15% otherwise, but the Canada-residence treaty and limitation-on-benefits or anti-abuse conditions must be checked. The Canada-United States treaty commonly provides 5% for a qualifying corporate parent owning at least 10% of voting power and 15% in other cases.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: Before payment or credit, obtain and retain a valid certificate of residence or equivalent reliable evidence, beneficial-owner information, ownership records, treaty eligibility, and any applicable limitation-on-benefits or principal-purpose analysis. The Canadian payer generally self-assesses the reduced rate and remits tax to the CRA; advance CRA approval is not ordinarily required for ordinary treaty-reduced dividends, interest, or royalties. Apply for a CRA waiver or reduction where a specific waiver procedure is required. Remit by the applicable due date, issue NR4 slips, and maintain records supporting the rate. If treaty relief is denied or over-withholding occurs, the recipient may pursue the applicable CRA refund or objection process.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic Part XIII rate is generally 25% on Canadian-source royalties and interest paid or credited to non-residents, subject to statutory exemptions and treaty relief. Treaty rates vary. Copyright, software, patent, trademark, film, and know-how royalties are commonly reduced to 0% or 10%, depending on the treaty and characterization. Arm's-length interest is commonly reduced to 0% under many Canadian treaties, including the Canada-United States treaty for qualifying interest, while some treaties provide 10% or another rate. Non-arm's-length interest may be subject to statutory exemptions only if detailed conditions are satisfied. Software payments must be analyzed as royalties, business profits, services, or mixed consideration; the contract and rights granted control the characterization.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canada has no general monetary threshold below which contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation is unnecessary. Under Income Tax Act section 247, contemporaneous documentation is required for non-arm's-length cross-border transactions with non-residents, and the documentation must generally be prepared by the return-filing deadline and provided to the CRA within three months of a written request. Form T106 generally applies where statutory reportable non-arm's-length non-resident transaction conditions are met, including the CAD 1,000,000 aggregate threshold for relevant transaction categories. Country-by-country reporting generally applies to a Canadian-resident ultimate parent or surrogate parent of an MNE group with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the preceding fiscal year. Canada does not impose a separate universal Local File or Master File threshold under a formal OECD-style filing regime, although CRA documentation should cover the substance of both concepts where relevant.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: Other method supported by reliable evidence where the listed methods are less appropriate
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no standalone general Economic Substance Regulations equivalent to certain offshore ESR regimes. Substance is enforced through the transfer-pricing arm's-length principle, the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, treaty anti-abuse provisions, beneficial-ownership analysis, sham and factual-reality doctrines, and source and residency rules. A Canadian game publisher should maintain Canadian decision-making, personnel, development or publishing functions, risk control, IP and contract records, bank-account control, and evidence supporting the actual functions performed. Conduit dividend, interest, or royalty structures with no genuine control or commercial purpose are high risk.
operational_transfer_pricing_requirement: Identify all cross-border related-party transactions, including game-development services, IP licenses, platform support, marketing, financing, royalties, cost sharing, reimbursements, and receivables.
Prepare a functional analysis covering functions performed, assets used, risks controlled, IP ownership, platform relationships, and economically significant personnel.
Select and apply the most appropriate method consistently; document tested party, comparables, adjustments, pricing period, and financial metrics.
Reconcile intercompany invoices, contracts, general ledger accounts, customs or payment data, T106 reporting, and withholding-tax returns.
Monitor year-end results and make only legally supportable true-up entries with proper invoices, withholding analysis, and accounting treatment.
Retain records for the statutory retention period and preserve platform statements, user-revenue reports, refunds, chargebacks, and foreign-exchange calculations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Tax Reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly concealing platform revenue, omitting Steam or console-store receipts, fabricating expenses, backdating related-party invoices, claiming fictitious SR&ED, or deliberately understating taxable income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the federal Income Tax Act, conviction can result in a fine generally ranging from 50% to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded and imprisonment for up to two years. Civil reassessment, interest, gross-negligence penalties, and denial of credits may also apply. Quebec may impose separate penalties and criminal consequences.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face personal criminal liability where they participated in or directed the offence. Corporate status does not protect intentional criminal conduct. Imprisonment is possible; travel restrictions may arise through criminal-process orders but are not an automatic tax sanction. Restitution or repayment may be ordered where legally available.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Withhold or Remit Non-Resident Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, royalties, interest, or other Part XIII amounts to a foreign parent, developer, or IP owner without applying the correct withholding rate, remitting by the deadline, or issuing NR4 slips.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation may be assessed for the unremitted tax, interest, and withholding penalties. Reduced treaty rates may be denied where residency, beneficial ownership, or treaty entitlement is unsupported.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be assessed personally for amounts deemed held in trust, including certain source deductions and statutory remittances, if the corporation failed to remit and the statutory due-diligence defence is unavailable.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register, collect, report, or remit GST/HST or QST on taxable digital supplies, incorrectly treating Canadian customers or platform settlements as outside scope, or claiming unsupported input tax credits or input tax refunds.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Assessment of uncollected tax, denial of credits, interest, gross-negligence penalties, late-filing penalties, and possible prosecution may result. Platform-facilitator collection rules must be analyzed separately from direct-sales obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can incur personal liability for certain GST/HST and QST amounts held in trust where statutory conditions are met. Liability may continue after dissolution or asset transfers.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Shifting Canadian publishing profit to a foreign IP owner through unsupported royalties, excessive management fees, non-arm's-length financing, or a contract that does not reflect actual functions and risks.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may reassess under section 247, impose a transfer-pricing penalty generally equal to 10% of the adjustment where the statutory conditions are met, deny deductions, impose withholding tax, and seek an extended reassessment period for serious misrepresentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not ordinarily personally liable merely because a transfer-pricing adjustment is made, but personal exposure can arise for knowing participation, false statements, source-remittance failures, or criminal tax conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Filing of T106, Foreign-Affiliate, or Country-by-Country Information
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to disclose reportable non-resident related-party transactions, foreign affiliates, or CbC information after the applicable threshold and filing conditions are met.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Specific fixed or formula-based information-return penalties may apply, together with extended audit periods, transfer-pricing penalties, denial of treaty positions, and compliance orders where available.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Ordinary information-return penalties are generally imposed on the corporation, but directors may be personally exposed for deliberate false filings or related trust and withholding failures.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company, Sham, or Treaty-Conduit Arrangement
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a nominal Canadian company with no genuine Canadian management or commercial activity to obtain treaty benefits, receive funds for immediate onward payment, or disguise the beneficial owner of IP, dividends, or financing.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may deny treaty relief under beneficial-ownership, anti-avoidance, principal-purpose, or GAAR principles, reassess tax, impose interest and penalties, and challenge the factual residence or commercial characterization of the arrangement.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face civil claims, tax assessments connected with statutory trust obligations, and criminal liability for fraud or tax evasion if they knowingly implemented the sham. There is no automatic corporate veil piercing solely because the entity has limited substance.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Corporate Dissolution or Asset Stripping Before Tax Clearance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Distributing cash, IP, or platform receivables to shareholders or foreign affiliates while tax, payroll, GST/HST, QST, or withholding liabilities remain unpaid.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax authorities may assess the corporation, challenge transfers, apply deemed-trust rules, pursue transferees under applicable statutory provisions, and impose interest and penalties. Dissolution does not extinguish pre-existing tax liabilities.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally assessed for source deductions, GST/HST, QST, and other trust amounts if statutory conditions are satisfied. Liability may arise despite resignation if the person was a director during the relevant period.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining incomplete records of Valve or console payouts, refunds, chargebacks, user geography, foreign-exchange conversions, intercompany settlements, or digital rights granted.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA or Revenu Québec may issue compliance demands, make indirect-method assessments, disallow deductions or credits, impose record-keeping penalties, and apply gross-negligence penalties where the evidentiary failure supports that conclusion.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face personal consequences for obstruction, false records, or trust-remittance failures. Ordinary poor bookkeeping alone does not automatically create unlimited personal liability.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Receiving or transmitting suspicious third-party funds, concealing beneficial owners, dealing with sanctioned persons, or using payment structures designed to evade Canadian sanctions or financial-reporting controls.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The ordinary game publisher is not automatically a FINTRAC reporting entity solely because it publishes software, but obligations can arise if it performs a regulated financial activity or operates as a money-services business. Sanctions breaches may result in administrative monetary penalties or criminal prosecution, including substantial fines and imprisonment under applicable Canadian legislation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers who authorize or knowingly permit sanctions evasion, money laundering, or false records may face criminal prosecution, asset seizure, fines, and imprisonment. Travel bans are not automatic but may arise from court orders or immigration consequences.
